blocks.p: A complete line can't be drawn on paper; what we draw is a segment with arrowheads showing it continues.
Three or more points on the same line are **collinear**. Three or more lines through the same single point are **concurrent**.

list: Given two distinct points, there is one and only one line through them.
Two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common.

sections.heading: Worked example: a ray standing on a line

blocks.p: If a ray stands on a line, the two adjacent angles it forms add up to $180^\circ$ (a linear pair). If those angles are $3x$ and $2x + 20^\circ$:
So the angles are $96^\circ$ and $84^\circ$, which do add to $180^\circ$.

How many line segments are determined by 5 points on a line? Each pair of points gives one segment, so there are $\dbinom{5}{2} = 10$. For 4 points with no three collinear, each pair also determines a different line: $\dbinom{4}{2} = 6$ lines.

list: 'A ray has a definite length.' **False.** It starts at one endpoint and goes on forever in one direction.
'Two distinct points determine exactly one line.' **True.** This is Euclid's axiom above.
'Any three points are collinear.' **False.** Three points are collinear only if one line passes through all of them.
**Naming a ray in the wrong order.** Ray $AB$ starts at $A$ and passes through $B$; ray $BA$ is different.
**Treating a segment as a line.** Two segments can fail to meet even when the lines containing them would.
**Forgetting the 180° rule** when angles sit on a straight line.

exam.note: The 2025-26 CBSE Class IX syllabus lists Euclid's geometry, including the axiom that two distinct points have one and only one line through them and the theorem that two distinct lines cannot have more than one point in common, and, under Lines and Angles, that if a ray stands on a line the two adjacent angles add up to 180°.
